title: LLM Inference Challenges -Understanding the Modern AI Inference Stack
author: Anurag Mohan

blocks.text: LLM Inference Challenges (Part 14)
Understanding CUDA, vLLM, CPU Inference, Model Routing, and Agentic AI
In the previous parts, we explored:

KV cache
batching
multi-GPU inference
distributed serving
GPU communication
prefill vs decode
continuous batching
PagedAttention
vLLM architecture
At this point, the inference system picture started becoming clearer. But then I started getting confused by another set of questions.

Where does CUDA fit? 
Where does PyTorch fit? 
Where does vLLM fit? 
Why are people suddenly talking about CPU inference? 
Does small model inference mean GPUs become less important? 
How does model routing work? 
Where do load balancers fit? 
And finally, where does Agentic AI fit in all of this?
This article is my attempt to connect all of these ideas into one mental model.
What is the first confusion?
The first confusion is usually this:

Is CUDA similar to vLLM?
Is PyTorch similar to CUDA?
Is vLLM doing the computation?
Is the GPU doing the computation?
These things are connected, but they are not the same layer.
What actually performs the computation?
The GPU performs the actual computation. The GPU is the hardware. It contains:

GPU cores
tensor cores
HBM memory
caches
When an LLM runs, the GPU performs operations like:

matrix multiplication
attention computation
tensor operations
So the GPU is the actual worker.
Then what is CUDA?

CUDA is NVIDIA’s software platform for programming NVIDIA GPUs. The GPU performs the computation. CUDA provides the software layer that allows programs to tell the GPU what to do. A simple mental model:

GPU = hardware that performs computation

CUDA = software layer used to control NVIDIA GPUs
CUDA helps with:

launching GPU kernels
moving data to GPU memory
running optimized GPU libraries
coordinating GPU execution
So CUDA is not replacing the GPU. CUDA is how software talks to the GPU.
What is PyTorch then?
PyTorch sits above CUDA. When we write:
torch.matmul(A, B)

we are not manually writing CUDA code. PyTorch handles the tensor operation at a higher level. Under the hood, PyTorch may call CUDA libraries, and CUDA then launches work on the GPU. So the stack looks like:

PyTorch
  ↓
CUDA
  ↓
GPU
PyTorch manages tensors and model execution. CUDA manages GPU execution. The GPU performs the actual math.
Where does vLLM fit?
vLLM sits even higher. vLLM is not mainly about writing matrix multiplication kernels. vLLM is an inference serving engine. It focuses on:

request scheduling
continuous batching
KV cache management
PagedAttention
prefill and decode execution
token streaming
serving many users efficiently
So vLLM is not competing with CUDA. vLLM uses lower-level systems underneath it. A simplified stack looks like:

Application
  ↓
vLLM
  ↓
PyTorch / CUDA kernels
  ↓
GPU
What is the simplest mental model?
I think about it like this:

GPU = does the math

CUDA = tells NVIDIA GPU how to do the math

PyTorch = expresses model computation using tensors

vLLM = manages inference serving for many requests
So when a user sends a prompt, vLLM is not personally multiplying every matrix. vLLM decides what should run and when. Then the model execution happens through lower-level compute layers.
What does vLLM actually manage?
Suppose many users send requests:

Request A
Request B
Request C
Request D
vLLM decides:

Which requests enter the batch?
Which requests wait?
Which requests are in prefill?
Which requests are in decode?
How much KV cache memory is available?
Which requests finished?
Which requests can be admitted next?
That is why I now think of vLLM as:
a runtime system for LLM inference
It is not just:
run model.generate()
It is more like:
manage many dynamic generation workloads efficiently
What is a useful analogy?

Imagine a restaurant. The GPU is the kitchen. CUDA is the kitchen equipment and controls. PyTorch is the chef who knows how to use the equipment. vLLM is the restaurant manager. The restaurant manager does not cook every dish directly. Instead, the manager decides:

which orders enter
which orders wait
which orders can be grouped
which tables need service
how to keep the kitchen busy
That is very similar to what vLLM does for inference.
Why did this matter before talking about CPU inference?
Because once the stack is clear, CPU inference becomes easier to understand. The question is not:
Can CUDA run on CPU?
CUDA is NVIDIA GPU-specific. The better question is:
Can LLM inference run on hardware other than GPUs?
And the answer is yes. Inference can run on:

GPU
CPU
NPU
integrated GPU
edge devices
But the engine and optimization strategy may change.
Why are people suddenly talking about inference on CPUs?
Because the industry is realizing something important:

Training is usually GPU-heavy.

Inference depends on the workload.
Training large models requires enormous compute. GPUs are extremely important there. But inference is different. Inference happens repeatedly, for every user request. So the question becomes:

Can this request be served cheaper?
Can it be served locally?
Can it be served with lower power?
Can it be served without sending data to the cloud?
That is where CPU inference and edge inference become interesting.
Does this mean CPUs are replacing GPUs?
No. That is not the right mental model. The shift is not:
GPU → CPU
The shift is:
Use the right hardware for the right inference workload.
Large models, large context windows, and high-throughput serving still heavily benefit from GPUs. But smaller models and simpler tasks may run well enough on CPUs or edge accelerators.
What changed to make CPU inference more practical?
A few things changed at the same time. First, smaller models became much better. Models like:

1B
3B
7B
8B
can now solve many practical tasks. Second, quantization became much better. Third, CPUs, NPUs, and local AI hardware became more capable. So now the question is not always:
Do we need the biggest model?
The question becomes:
What is the smallest model that can solve this task well enough?
What is quantization again?
A model is mostly weights. Weights are numbers. For example:
If we store each number in FP16, each weight takes:
16 bits = 2 bytes
So a 7B model in FP16 needs roughly:
7 billion × 2 bytes ≈ 14 GB
just for weights.
What does quantization do?
Quantization stores approximate versions of those weights using fewer bits. Instead of:
FP16
we may use:

INT8
INT4
So memory can shrink like:

FP16 → 16 bits per weight
INT8 → 8 bits per weight
INT4 → 4 bits per weight
A rough mental model:

14 GB in FP16
≈ 7 GB in INT8
≈ 3.5 GB in INT4
This is one reason smaller models can run on laptops, desktops, and CPU servers.
Why does quality not completely collapse?
Because neural networks are often tolerant to small approximation errors. If a weight changes from:
to:

the model may still behave similarly. Of course, there is a tradeoff. More aggressive quantization can reduce quality. But for many workloads, the quality loss is acceptable compared to the gain in cost, memory, and deployment flexibility.
Does a small LLM work as well as a large LLM?
Not always. This is important. A small model is not universally as good as a large model. But for many tasks, a small model may be good enough. Examples:

simple summarization
classification
basic Q&A
routing decisions
template-based assistance
local assistant tasks
For harder reasoning, long context, coding, research, or complex analysis, a larger model may still be needed. So the question becomes:
Which model is good enough for this request?
This leads directly to model routing.
What is model routing?
Model routing means the system decides which model should handle a request. Instead of:
All requests → Large LLM
we get:

Request
  ↓
Router
  ↓
Best model for this request
For example:

Simple question
  ↓
Small model on CPU

Complex reasoning
  ↓
Large model on GPU

Research task
  ↓
Specialized research model

Document understanding
  ↓
Document AI service
The goal is:

Use the cheapest model and hardware
that can still produce a good answer.
Is this similar to what we learned about replicas?
Yes, but at a different level. Earlier we learned:

Load Balancer
  ↓
Replica 1
Replica 2
Replica 3
That was mostly about distributing requests across replicas of the same service. Model routing is higher level. It asks:
Which service or model should handle this request?
Then load balancing happens inside that chosen service.
Does vLLM do this routing?
Usually, no. vLLM has an internal scheduler. That scheduler decides:

which requests run now
which requests wait
how batching works
how KV cache is allocated
But vLLM is usually not the outer system deciding:

Should this request go to a CPU model?
Should it go to a GPU model?
Should it go to a research model?
Should it go to a document model?
That outer decision is usually handled by a router or AI gateway above the inference engine.
So does the router replace the load balancer?
No. This was an important clarification for me. The router and the load balancer solve different problems. The router decides:
WHAT should handle the request?
The load balancer decides:
WHERE exactly should the request go?
So the router chooses the service. The load balancer chooses the replica.
What does this architecture look like?
A useful production mental model is:

User
  ↓
API Gateway
  ↓
AI Router
  ├── Small Model Service
  │       ↓
  │   Load Balancer
  │       ↓
  │   CPU Replicas
  │
  ├── Large LLM Service
  │       ↓
  │   Load Balancer
  │       ↓
  │   GPU Replicas
  │
  ├── Research Model Service
  │       ↓
  │   Load Balancer
  │       ↓
  │   GPU Replicas
  │
  └── Document Understanding Service
          ↓
      Load Balancer
          ↓
      Replicas

This matches the mental model I was trying to build. The router is not simply replacing the load balancer. The router sits above multiple model services. Each service may still have its own load balancer and replicas.
What does the router use to make decisions?
The router may use:

rules
metadata
prompt length
user tier
cost limits
privacy requirements
latency targets
model availability
It may also use a small model or classifier. For example:

Request
  ↓
Small router model
  ↓
Classify request complexity
  ↓
Choose destination
What is a model cascade?
A cascade means we try a cheaper model first. If it is confident, return the answer. If it is not confident, escalate. Example:

Request
  ↓
Small model

Confident?
  ↓
Return answer

Not confident?
  ↓
Send to larger model
This can reduce cost because not every request needs the largest model.
What routers do people use in practice?
Many companies build custom routers. Common approaches include:

rule-based routing
classifier-based routing
semantic routing
confidence-based cascades
AI gateways
There are also products and projects in this space, such as:

LiteLLM
Portkey
Semantic Router style systems
custom internal gateways
But the important idea is not the specific tool. The important idea is the layer:

a routing layer sits above model endpoints
and decides where each request should go
How does this connect to CPU inference?
CPU inference becomes useful when the router has cheaper destinations available. For example:

Simple request
  ↓
Small quantized model
  ↓
CPU inference service
A more complex request may go to:

Large model
  ↓
GPU inference service
So CPU inference is not necessarily replacing GPU inference. It becomes one more option in the routing system.
What does a CPU inference service look like?
A CPU inference service may still have:

API endpoint
request queue
scheduler
batching
KV cache
replicas
load balancer
So many inference concepts still apply. But the hardware constraints are different.
What is different about CPU inference?
A GPU usually has:

very high parallel compute
very high memory bandwidth
limited HBM capacity
A CPU server may have:

less parallel compute
larger system RAM
lower cost
simpler deployment
So CPU inference is often attractive for:

small models
quantized models
low-throughput workloads
local inference
edge inference
privacy-sensitive tasks
Does everything we learned apply only to GPU clusters?
No. Some ideas are universal. For example:

request routing
load balancing
batching
scheduling
KV cache
replicas
latency vs throughput
These apply to CPU and GPU inference. But some ideas are much more GPU-specific:

CUDA
tensor parallelism
pipeline parallelism across GPUs
NCCL
NVLink
GPU communication
TensorRT-LLM
So the higher-level inference system concepts apply broadly. The low-level optimization details depend on the hardware.
Can vLLM run on CPU?
vLLM is mostly known for high-throughput GPU serving. But vLLM also has CPU backend support. However, the reason vLLM became popular is strongly connected to:

continuous batching
PagedAttention
GPU memory efficiency
high-throughput serving
So while vLLM can be used with CPUs in some cases, most people associate vLLM with GPU inference systems.
Can TensorRT-LLM run on CPU?

TensorRT-LLM is different. TensorRT-LLM is NVIDIA’s optimized LLM inference stack for NVIDIA GPUs. So this is much more GPU-specific. If the system is CPU-only, TensorRT-LLM is usually not the right tool.
What do people use for CPU inference then?
This is where llama.cpp becomes important. llama.cpp is widely used for running LLMs locally and efficiently, especially quantized models. It is common in:

local inference
CPU inference
edge inference
laptop inference
small model experimentation
Tools like Ollama made this local inference experience much easier for many users. A simple mental model:

vLLM → production GPU serving

TensorRT-LLM → optimized NVIDIA GPU inference

llama.cpp → local / CPU-friendly / quantized inference

Ollama → easy local model running experience
Why is llama.cpp important?
Because it helped make local LLM inference practical. Instead of needing a large GPU cluster, users can run smaller quantized models on:

laptops
desktops
CPU servers
edge devices
This connects directly to the broader CPU inference discussion. If a model can fit in local memory and run fast enough, then not every request has to go to the cloud.
What is edge inference?
Edge inference means running inference close to the user or device. Instead of:

User
  ↓
Cloud GPU
  ↓
Response
we may have:

User
  ↓
Local device
  ↓
CPU / NPU / integrated GPU
  ↓
Response
This can help with:

latency
privacy
offline usage
cost
What role do NPUs play?
An NPU is a neural processing unit. A simple mental model:

CPU = general purpose compute

GPU = massively parallel compute

NPU = low-power AI acceleration
Many modern devices now include CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs together. So future inference may not be only cloud GPU inference. It may be a mix of:

local CPU
local NPU
local GPU
cloud GPU
How would routing work at the edge?
This is where the architecture becomes very interesting. Imagine a laptop or phone with a local router. A request arrives:
Summarize this email
The router may decide:

Small local model is enough
  ↓
Run locally
Another request arrives:

Analyze this long legal contract
and identify business risks
The router may decide:

Too complex for local model
  ↓
Send to cloud GPU model
So edge inference may use the same routing idea:

local if possible
cloud if needed
Why are people talking about CPUs, ARM, Intel, Dell, and AI PCs?
Because inference is no longer only about giant GPU clusters. There is a growing need to run AI across many types of hardware:

cloud GPUs
CPU servers
AI PCs
phones
edge devices
enterprise servers

Chip companies, server companies, and device companies all become relevant because inference workloads may spread across the entire compute stack. This does not mean GPUs become unimportant. It means inference becomes more distributed and more workload-specific.
Where does Agentic AI fit in all of this?
This was another major clarification for me. Agents are usually not LLMs themselves. Agents are orchestration systems. They sit above model calls. A simple stack looks like:

User
  ↓
Agent Runtime
  ↓
Router
  ↓
LLM Endpoint
  ↓
Inference Engine
  ↓
Hardware
The agent decides what needs to be done. The router decides which model or service should handle it. The inference engine generates tokens. The hardware runs the computation.
What does an agent actually do?
Suppose the user asks:

Find last month’s invoices
and summarize unusual expenses.
An agent may:

call accounting system
retrieve invoice data
call search tool
call LLM for analysis
call database
generate final answer

The agent is coordinating a workflow. It may call an LLM multiple times. It may call tools. It may store intermediate state. It may decide the next step based on previous results. But the agent itself is usually just software running on CPU.
Does an agent need a GPU?
Usually, no. The agent orchestration layer is often:

Python service
Java service
Node service
workflow runtime
This can run on CPUs. The GPU is needed when the system performs actual model inference on a GPU-backed model. So:

Agent orchestration = usually CPU

LLM inference = CPU, GPU, NPU, or cloud endpoint
How do agents and routing work together?
An agent may decide:
I need to call a model now.
Then the routing layer decides:
Which model should be called?
For example:

Agent needs simple classification
  ↓
Small CPU model

Agent needs deep reasoning
  ↓
Large GPU model

Agent needs document extraction
  ↓
Document model service

Agent needs local private answer
  ↓
Local model
So agents and routers solve different problems. The agent decides the workflow. The router chooses the model endpoint.
What does the full modern AI stack look like?
A more complete picture now looks like:

User
  ↓
API Gateway
  ↓
Agent Layer
  ↓
Model Router
  ├── Small CPU Model Service
  ├── Local Edge Model
  ├── Large GPU Model Service
  ├── Research Model Service
  └── Document Understanding Service
        ↓
     Load Balancer
        ↓
     Replicas
        ↓
     Inference Engine
        ↓
     Hardware
This is much bigger than just:
User → LLM
What is the difference between agent, router, load balancer, and inference engine?
This is the cleanest separation I now have:

Agent
= decides what steps need to happen

Router
= decides which model/service should handle a model call

Load Balancer
= decides which replica inside that service gets the request

Inference Engine
= runs the model efficiently

Hardware
= performs the computation
So:

Agent decides the workflow.

Router decides the destination.

Load balancer decides the replica.

Inference engine manages execution.

Hardware does the math.
How does this connect back to vLLM?
vLLM sits inside the inference service. For example:

Large LLM Service
  ↓
Load Balancer
  ↓
vLLM Replica
  ↓
GPU Workers
The outer router may choose the Large LLM Service. The load balancer may choose a specific vLLM replica. Then vLLM manages:

scheduling
continuous batching
PagedAttention
KV cache
prefill
decode
token generation
So vLLM is not the whole AI platform. It is a critical part of the inference layer.
What is the biggest mental shift?
Earlier, I was mostly thinking about:

one model
many requests
Now the picture is more like:

many models
many hardware types
many services
many workflows
This changes the architecture. The system is no longer only asking:
How do we run this model efficiently?
It is also asking:

Should this request run locally?
Should it use a small model?
Should it use a large model?
Should it use CPU?
Should it use GPU?
Should it call a tool first?
Should an agent break it into steps?
What is the key intuition?
The modern inference stack is becoming layered. At the bottom:
CPU / GPU / NPU
Above that:
CUDA / CPU kernels / hardware runtime
Above that:
PyTorch / llama.cpp / TensorRT-LLM / other execution layers
Above that:
vLLM / inference engine / serving runtime
Above that:
load balancer
Above that:
model router
Above that:
agent workflow
So the full system is not just about generating tokens. It is about deciding:

what to do
which model to use
where to run it
how to serve it efficiently
how to keep cost and latency under control
What does this teach us about CPU inference?
CPU inference is not a separate universe. It is one part of a larger inference platform. For some requests:
CPU + small quantized model
may be enough. For others:
GPU + large model
is needed. For local tasks:
edge model
may be best. For complex workflows:
agent + tools + multiple model calls
may be required. So the future is not:
CPU vs GPU
It is:
CPU + GPU + NPU + routing + agents
working together.
What comes next?
This article helped me connect several pieces:

CUDA
PyTorch
vLLM
CPU inference
GPU inference
quantization
llama.cpp
model routing
load balancers
edge inference
Agentic AI
The next natural step is to go deeper into CPU and local inference. That probably means exploring:

llama.cpp
GGUF models
quantized inference
Ollama
local model serving
CPU vs GPU performance tradeoffs
Because now the high-level architecture is clearer. The next question becomes:
How does local CPU inference actually work in practice?
